findings.summary: In the "Which Tool?" flowchart the edge labels "recover" and "shared branch" are drawn on top of the node boxes, making the node labels "cherry-pick" and "bisect" unreadable.
findings.evidence: Second row of the diagram renders "recover" struck across the green node whose label is "cherry-pick", and "shared branch" printed across the blue node whose label is "bisect"; both node labels are obscured mid-word while the nodes below ("reflog", "revert") are clean.
findings.fix: Move the "recover" and "shared branch" edge labels off the node boxes — place them beside their connector lines (as "copy" and "hunt" are on the row above) or increase vertical spacing between the decision diamond and the cherry-pick/bisect node row so labels sit on the connectors, not on the nodes.

findings.summary: The part opens with an advanced `git bisect start --first-parent` snippet before bisect is introduced anywhere in this part and before the page's own numbered section 1.
findings.evidence: First block of page 1: code `git bisect start --first-parent` / `# answer: 'merge #412 is bad'` / `# then bisect inside that merge`, note "faster search, coarser answer" — it precedes the heading "1. Cherry-pick Flags" and the heading "2. Bisect & Reflog Recap".
findings.fix: Move the `--first-parent` code block under "2. Bisect & Reflog Recap", after the bisect command table that establishes `bisect start HEAD v1.9`, so the coarser-but-faster variant follows the baseline session.

findings.summary: The "anti-pattern" takeaway is asserted as the second block, before the trade-off table below it and the worked example on page 2 that supply its only evidence.
findings.evidence: Page 1 block 2: "Cherry-pick is a **patch courier**, not a branch strategy. Long-lived branches need merges" — the supporting "conflict cost / every branch" row appears later in section 3, and the concrete case ("Release 2.4 gets 14 cherry-picks from main. What breaks in month three?") is on page 2.
findings.fix: Relocate the anti-pattern callout to directly after the trade-off table in section 3 (or to the end of page 2's worked example), so the conclusion follows the data that earns it.

findings.summary: The worked example attributes duplicate-patch detection during `git merge` to patch-id, but merge is a content-level three-way merge that never computes patch-ids.
findings.evidence: "`git merge main` re-offers all 14 patches" / "Patch-id drops only __byte-identical__ ones; conflict-resolved picks stay"
findings.fix: Rewrite the mechanism: merge diffs both sides against the merge base, so picks whose content matches upstream merge cleanly and produce no re-application, while picks that were edited/conflict-resolved show up as conflicts. Move the patch-id caveat to where it actually applies — `git cherry`, `git rebase`, and `git am -3`, which skip commits whose patch-id already exists upstream.

findings.summary: Patch-id equivalence is described as requiring byte-identical patches, but git patch-id ignores line numbers and (in the default --stable mode) all whitespace and file reordering.
findings.fix: Change to: "patch-id ignores line numbers, whitespace and file order — a pick that landed at a different offset still matches; only picks whose content actually changed during conflict resolution stay." (git-patch-id docs: "a sum of SHA-1 of the file diffs ... with line numbers ignored"; --stable: "All whitespace within the patch is ignored".)

findings.summary: Section numbering on page 2 is broken: it opens with "5. Worked Example" and then restarts at 2, so the number 5 appears twice and out of order.
findings.evidence: Page 2 headings in order: "5. Worked Example", "2. Find What To Pick", "3. Bisect Session", "4. Reflog Selectors", "5. Undo and Rescue", "6. Search Instead of Bisect".
findings.fix: Renumber the opening block to "1. Worked Example" so the page reads 1→6 and the single "5" is "5. Undo and Rescue", which page 3's "7. Safety and Config" then continues.

findings.summary: "Patch-id" is used as load-bearing terminology in the worked example before the only line that explains it, one section later.
findings.evidence: Section "5. Worked Example": "Patch-id drops only __byte-identical__ ones; conflict-resolved picks stay" — the explanation "`git cherry` matches by patch-id" appears afterwards as the note on "2. Find What To Pick".
findings.fix: Add a half-line gloss at first use in the worked example (e.g. "patch-id = a hash of the diff text itself") or move the `git cherry` section ahead of the worked example.

findings.summary: The destructive-triad table says nothing uncommitted survives `reset --hard`, but content that was staged is written to the object database and is recoverable as a dangling blob.
findings.evidence: "`reset --hard`","tree + index + HEAD","**commits** yes via reflog — uncommitted tree/index ==no=="
findings.fix: Split the cell: commits → reflog; staged (added) content → recoverable as dangling blobs via `git fsck --lost-found` until gc prunes them; never-staged working-tree edits → gone. This also ties into the `git fsck --unreachable` rescue line on the same page.

findings.summary: The safety block presents `gc.reflogExpire 90.days` (and the 30-day unreachable value) as protective settings to apply, but both are already Git's defaults, so the command changes nothing.
findings.evidence: "git config gc.reflogExpire 90.days" and "`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable=30.days` — orphans die sooner"
findings.fix: Bump the example above the default to make it a real safety change (e.g. `git config gc.reflogExpire 180.days` and `git config gc.reflogExpireUnreachable 90.days`), and label 90 days / 30 days explicitly as the shipped defaults rather than as settings you apply.
